title: The Nairobi Hospital School of Nursing September 2011 Class GIT Disorders End of Block I Examination

sets.title: Set 1: Original Exam Questions
sets.description: The original MCQs and True/False statements from The Nairobi Hospital School of Nursing September 2011 class GIT Disorders End of Block I Examination paper (GIT Disorders, sat 20 June 2012, Part A, Q1 to Q10).

questions.text: Increased gastric acid secretion is common in the following condition:
questions.explanation: Duodenal ulcers (B) is correct because patients with duodenal ulcers typically have hypersecretion of gastric acid (an increased parietal cell mass, raised gastrin response and rapid gastric emptying that delivers acid to the duodenum), and H. pylori infection also adds to the damage. Gastric ulcers (A) is incorrect because acid secretion is normal or low in gastric ulcers, and the main problem is a weakened mucosal barrier. Hiatal hernia (C) is incorrect because the problem is the displacement of the stomach through the diaphragm and not the acid output. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (D) is incorrect because it is due to an incompetent lower esophageal sphincter and not to excess acid secretion.

questions.text: Cancer of the esophagus has a poor prognosis due to:

options.A: Liver or lung metastases are usually present before diagnosis is made
options.B: The tumor is radio resistant and inaccessible to surgery

questions.explanation: Liver or lung metastases are usually present before diagnosis is made (A) is correct from the options because the early symptoms are minimal (dysphagia appears only when the lumen is about two thirds blocked), so the patient presents late, and because the esophagus lacks a serosal layer and has a rich lymphatic drainage, the cancer spreads early to the lymph nodes, liver and lungs. The tumor is radio resistant and inaccessible to surgery (B) is incorrect because esophageal tumours respond to radiotherapy and chemotherapy and surgery (esophagectomy) is done in early disease. The cancer is usually undifferentiated (C) is incorrect because most are squamous cell carcinomas or adenocarcinomas. Local spread prevents complete removal (D) is incorrect as the best answer, although local invasion of adjacent structures does limit resection. Note: option D is also a recognised reason, so check this item against the marking scheme.

questions.text: Substernal pressure after 2-3 seconds of solid food ingestion and lower esophageal sphincter constriction following manometry studies is suggestive of:
questions.explanation: Achalasia (C) is correct because in achalasia the lower esophageal sphincter does not relax when the patient swallows (it stays constricted and has a high resting pressure on manometry) and there is no peristalsis in the esophageal body, so food is held up and causes a feeling of substernal pressure or fullness seconds after swallowing. Esophageal varices (A) is incorrect because they are dilated veins that cause painless bleeding (hematemesis). Oropharyngeal dysphagia (B) is incorrect because the difficulty is in starting the swallow at once (the food cannot be passed from the mouth to the esophagus), with choking and aspiration. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (D) is incorrect because the sphincter is weak and relaxes inappropriately, and the manometry shows a low sphincter pressure.

options.D: Administration of high fibre, low fat diet

questions.explanation: Administration of high fibre, low fat diet (D) is correct because a high-fibre diet (with plenty of fluids) makes the stool bulky and soft, so it passes easily and lowers the pressure inside the colon, which prevents the formation of more diverticula and their inflammation (diverticulitis); a low-fat diet is also advised. Administration of opioid analgesics (A) is incorrect because opioids slow bowel movement, cause constipation and raise the pressure in the colon. Administration of stimulant laxatives (B) is incorrect because they cause cramping and raise the colonic pressure; bulk-forming agents are used instead. Encouraging patient to ambulate (C) is incorrect because it is a general measure and is not the main management of the condition.

questions.text: Risk factor to development of stress ulcers include:
questions.explanation: Long term mechanical ventilation (D) is correct because stress ulcers occur in critically ill patients who have severe physiological stress, such as shock, sepsis, burns (Curling's ulcer), head injury (Cushing's ulcer), major trauma, and respiratory failure needing prolonged ventilation, which reduces blood flow to the gastric mucosa and weakens the mucosal barrier. Zollinger Ellison syndrome (A) is incorrect because it causes ulcers through gastrin-driven acid hypersecretion, and these are not called stress ulcers. Psychological stress (B) is incorrect because stress ulcers are caused by physiological stress of severe illness and not by emotional stress. Respiratory distress syndrome (C) is incorrect as the best answer because it is the long ventilation and the critical illness that carry the risk. Note: option B is also a plausible reading of the word stress, so check this item against the marking scheme.

questions.text: An AIDS patient develops persistent diarrhea without blood in faeces, the most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Parasitic infestation (C) is correct because chronic watery diarrhoea without blood is very common in patients with AIDS and is most often caused by opportunistic intestinal parasites and protozoa such as Cryptosporidium, Isospora and Microsporidia (and also by Giardia, Cytomegalovirus and Mycobacterium avium complex), because of the weak immunity. Stress disorder (A) is incorrect because it does not cause persistent diarrhoea. Intestinal lymphoma (B) is incorrect as the most likely cause because, although it occurs in AIDS, it is much less common and often presents with pain, obstruction or bleeding. Enterocarcinoma (D) is incorrect because it is a cancer of the intestinal lining that is rare in this setting and usually presents with bleeding or obstruction.

questions.text: The best treatment in an elderly female who has increasing difficulty in swallowing which has developed gradually with no other systemic symptoms is:
questions.explanation: Dilatation by instrumentation (C) is correct because gradually increasing difficulty in swallowing without weight loss or other systemic symptoms in an elderly woman suggests a benign stricture or web of the esophagus (for example a peptic stricture or a Plummer-Vinson web), and this is relieved by passing a dilator (bougie or balloon) through the narrowed area. Radiotherapy (A), chemotherapy (B) and radical esophagectomy (D) are incorrect because they are treatments for esophageal cancer, which is not likely here because there are no systemic symptoms such as weight loss and the course is slow and not malignant. Note: the paper listed a blank fifth option (e) for this question, which has been ignored.

questions.text: The following occurs in chronic pancreatitis:

options.A: Decrease in fasting blood glucose levels

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 malabsorption (B) is correct because in chronic pancreatitis the destruction of the gland causes exocrine insufficiency; the lack of pancreatic proteases means that vitamin B12 is not released from its binding protein (R-protein) and so is not absorbed, and fat and protein malabsorption cause steatorrhoea and weight loss. Decrease in fasting blood glucose levels (A) is incorrect because the loss of islet cells causes diabetes mellitus, so the fasting glucose rises. Increased levels of serum amylase (C) is incorrect because the amylase is usually normal or only mildly raised in chronic pancreatitis, since the gland is fibrosed and has little enzyme left to release (it is raised in acute attacks). Increased levels of alkaline phosphatase (D) is incorrect as the best answer, although it may rise if the bile duct is compressed by the swollen pancreatic head. Note: option D is also possible, so check this item against the marking scheme.

questions.text: Administration of lactulose in hepatic encephalopathy helps in:
questions.explanation: Decreasing the colon pH (A) is correct because lactulose is broken down by colonic bacteria into lactic and acetic acids, which lower the pH of the colon; the acid environment converts ammonia (NH3) into ammonium (NH4+), which is not absorbed and is trapped in the bowel, so it is lost in the stool, and the laxative effect also removes the nitrogenous waste. Ammonia absorption (B) is incorrect because lactulose reduces and does not increase the absorption of ammonia. Urea formation (C) is incorrect because the liver forms urea from ammonia, and lactulose does not do this. Protein formation (D) is incorrect because lactulose does not help to build protein, and protein intake is actually restricted in severe encephalopathy.

questions.text: In appendicitis, there is lower left quadrant pain following Right lower quadrant palpation.
questions.explanation: False (B) is correct because the classic sign is the reverse of this statement: in Rovsing's sign, palpation of the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant, because gas and pressure are shifted towards the inflamed appendix and irritate the peritoneum. In appendicitis the tenderness is localised at McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant, and pain in the left lower quadrant after pressing on the right side is not the recognised finding. Note: the statement may have been meant as Rovsing's sign, so check this item against the marking scheme.

questions.text: In liver assessment, spider angiomas are palpated.
questions.explanation: False (B) is correct because spider angiomas (spider nevi) are small red vascular lesions with radiating branches, usually seen on the face, neck, shoulders and upper chest in liver disease (from raised estrogen levels), and they are inspected and not palpated; the nurse presses on the centre and they blanch. The liver itself is palpated for size, edge and tenderness.
